chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan ibn Yahya and Fadala ibn Ayyub from al-Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of them (peace be upon them both)

Regarding a man who arrives from the absence (ghaybah) and the time for prayer enters upon him, he said: 'If he does not fear that the time will expire, let him enter (the house) and complete (the prayer); and if he fears that the time will expire before he enters, let him pray and shorten (it).'

So it was inferred from this news that whoever does not fear missing the time by delaying the prayer until he enters the house, he delays it until he performs it completely; for if missing the time were not considered in this matter, there would be no meaning in restricting the completion to this state.

Al-Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And the traveler should not lead the resident, nor the resident lead the traveler. The preferable and best is that the traveler does not pray behind the resident, nor the resident behind the traveler. If they do that, they leave the preference, but their prayer is valid. And whenever the traveler prays behind the resident, he prays two rak'ahs and departs. And when the traveler prays with the people, he prays two rak'ahs with them, then he appoints someone to complete the prayer for them, and he (the traveler) departs. And that which indicates what we mentioned is what they narrated.

key_terms.اَلْغَيْبَةِ: Absence (often referring to the Minor or Major Occultation of the Imam)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a traveler arriving during prayer time and leading prayer as a traveler or resident?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the principle of *ikhtiyar* (choice) for a traveler arriving late, allowing them to either delay entry to complete the prayer or shorten it to ensure timely performance. It further clarifies the jurisprudence of *imamah* between travelers and residents, noting that while mutual leadership is valid, it is preferable for each to lead their own group to maintain ritual propriety. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on balancing ease (*rukhas*) with the preservation of prayer's structural integrity.
